reference_summary: At 09:22, a synthetic tree branch contacted feeder 47's primary conductor, causing relay 52-47 to open. The SCADA operator at Synthetic Control initiated remote closing of feeder breaker 52-47 at 09:31 after repairs were reported complete. The ground relay 51G-47's pickup was set to 150 amperes, while the magnetizing inrush produced 1.9 kiloamperes. Relay 27-47's undervoltage block was configured to release after 1 second, matching the dead-line check time exactly. After the 1.9 kiloampere inrush exceeded pickup, relay 51G-47 issued a trip command in 45 milliseconds. The distribution management system locked out feeder 47, stopping the restoration sequence and blocking remote closure. The failed restoration left 1,400 Synthetic customers without power for three hours, undercounted as a 12 megawatt-hour outage. No physical equipment was damaged because the 200 millisecond backup interrupter removed the false fault before thermal stress. Engineers uploaded corrected settings to relay 51G-47, raising pickup to 500 amperes with harmonic restraint enabled. Only if a zero-voltage check remains true for 20 seconds will breaker 52-47 reclose after a lockout.

reference_summary: At 13:05, lightning struck Synthetic North Feeder 9, causing a phase-to-phase fault and tripping the feeder breaker. After a successful 80 second dead-line test, operators issued an automatic restoration sequence at 14:22. The neutral overcurrent relay 51N-9 had a pickup of 240 amperes, which is less than the capacitor inrush. The restoration logic allowed breaker 52-9 to close while bus residual voltage remained at 35 percent. The 780 ampere capacitor inrush created a net neutral current of 620 amperes through relay 51N-9. Because 620 amperes exceeded the 240 ampere pickup, recloser R-9 locked out after only two fast operations. Synthetic North Feeder 9's 2,050 customers remained without power for 2.7 hours due to the failed restoration. No capacitor damage occurred because the bank fuse rated at 1,200 amperes did not melt under the 780 ampere inrush. Maintenance staff raised relay 51N-9's pickup to 800 amperes and enabled capacitor switching restraint logic. Only if bus residual voltage decays to zero for 30 seconds will breaker 52-9 be permitted to close.

reference_summary: The controller's software contained a start setpoint of 85°C instead of 75°C for the forced cooling groups. The primary pump motor overload relay was set to trip at 38 A, lower than the motor's rated 40 A. On 2026-09-08, the ambient air temperature reached 45°C and stayed there for eight hours. The grid dispatcher raised the transformer export loading to 108% of nameplate. In automatic sequence, the controller started the backup fan, whose zero-pitch blades produced negligible airflow. The transformer's top oil temperature climbed from 85°C to 96°C during the next twenty minutes. The transformer isolated from the grid at 15:27, leaving the synthetic polymer plant without power. After the event, laboratory analysis ruled out any overvoltage; thermal aging alone had cracked the bushings. A calibration service corrected the controller's temperature setpoint to the design value of 75°C. The motor overload relay was replaced and set with a trip current of 40 A.

reference_summary: The PLC watchdog timer had a 10 ms timeout, but its actual program scan period was 18 ms. Contaminants on the temperature sensing element created a constant negative offset of 7°C. On September 8, the ambient temperature remained above 42°C for 10 hours, adding heat input. A system instruction ordered transformer loading to 115% for the afternoon peak. Transformer oil, already heated by the 115% load and 45°C ambient, reached a top temperature of 96°C. With the sensor offset, the controller read 89°C while the true top oil temperature was 96°C. The transformer's internal pressure opened the spring relief valve at 15:20, disconnecting the unit. The post-trip inspection found no shorted turns in the windings; heat had softened the insulating paper. Adjusted the PLC watchdog to 25 ms and disabled automatic self-test during loaded operation. Cleaned and recalibrated the temperature sensor, effectively removing the constant 7°C offset.

reference_summary: The 11 kV cable at Synthetic West had no protective concrete slab above its route. A detailed drawing claimed an 80 cm depth, but the actual cable was buried at 42 cm. No lightning discharge occurred; nevertheless, the live cable was struck by an auger bit. The auger's cutting tooth deeply gouged the cable's lead sheath and wrappings. The cable current swelled to 3.2 kA and tripped the overcurrent relay after a short time. The overcurrent relay sent a trip signal to the circuit breaker at the feeder's remote end. The essential lighting switched to emergency lamps that were not designed for full duty. Data terminal displays flickered when the DC control voltage dipped to 104 V. A 200 kVA mobile generator, brought from a nearby store, fed the essential AC bus at 16:45. With temporary power available, workers tested the cable and found the auger cut location.
title: Auxiliary Power Failure at Synthetic West Substation Caused by Excavation Damage to Cable

reference_summary: The zone 1 impedance setting of the protection relay was 6.0 ohms, while the actual line impedance was 12.5 ohms. The automation logic lacked a directional check for distinguishing a reverse fault from a forward fault. A lightning bolt struck the Synthetic Alpine feeder conductor at 14:23, creating a phase-to-ground fault. A second lightning stroke at 14:25 initiated a phase-to-phase fault on the same feeder. Because of the incorrect setting, the relay erroneously localized the phase-to-ground fault to the distant line section. The erroneous localization produced a trip signal that opened the healthy loop tie sectionalizer, not the faulty one. Approximately 300 customers were without power for 210 minutes after the healthy lateral was misisolated. The repeated overcurrents shortened the life of the main line cable by an estimated 4.5 years. Protection engineers calibrated the relay distance zone to match the actual 12.5-ohm loop impedance. The automation firmware was upgraded to include a directional angle blocking element for fault isolation.

reference_summary: The Ethernet link between Synthetic Creek and Synthetic Lake had a latency of 800 ms, exceeding the automation's 100 ms limit. The loop restoration logic did not have a voltage check before closing the tie switch. At 15:12, snow accretion caused a conductor sag and a phase-to-phase contact on Synthetic Feeder 9. A lightning storm later caused an insulator flashover at Synthetic Creek, creating a second ground fault. If the link latency exceeds 100 ms, the controller falsely interprets the feeder as lost and issues a sectionalizer open command. The healthy sectionalizer opened, isolating a large commercial load but allowing a reverse power flow to a distributed generator. A total of 1,200 customers lost service for 2.5 hours due to the open sectionalizer and the tie close shock. The circulating current caused thermal damage to the bus bar and a subsequent transformer overcurrent. Engineers reduced the communication latency by installing fiber optic links instead of the old copper network. The loop restoration software was updated to include a voltage synchronism check before any tie switch close.
title: Synthetic Creek and Synthetic Lake Loop Restoration Failure in Snowstorm
